docs.title: Ireland – SPHE: Legal Framework and Regulatory Context (2023–2025)
1. Overview of the Irish Education System
1.1 Key Facts
docs.text: Parameter Value Country Ireland (IE) Population ~5.1 million (2024) Official languages Irish (Gaeilge), English Education system type Centralised curriculum, decentralised delivery (school autonomy on ethos) Compulsory schooling age 6–16 years Primary school Junior Infants (age 4/5) to 6th Class (age 11/12) – 8 years Junior Cycle (post-primary) 1st Year to 3rd Year (age 12–15) – 3 years; leads to Junior Cycle Profile of Achievement (JCPA) Senior Cycle (post-primary) 4th Year (Transition Year, optional) + 5th–6th Year (age 15–18) – 2 years; leads to Leaving Certificate Curriculum authority National Council for Curriculum and Assessment (NCCA) Department responsible Department of Education Ireland

docs.title: 1.2 Governance Structure
docs.text:
The Irish education system operates through:

  • Department of Education – sets national policy, statutory legislation, funding
  • NCCA (National Council for Curriculum and Assessment) – develops and reviews curriculum specifications; advises the Minister
  • Oide – professional learning and development service for teachers (formed from merger of PDST, JCT, and other services in 2022)
  • Schools – implement curriculum with significant autonomy regarding ethos, timetabling, and implementation approach
  • Parents – retain the right to opt children out of specific content that contravenes their conscience

docs.title: 2.1 Origins (1999–2010)
docs.text: Date Development 1999 SPHE introduced at primary level as part of the revised primary curriculum 2000–2001 SPHE introduced at post-primary Junior Cycle level 2003 RSE (Relationships and Sexuality Education) established as part of SPHE 2006 Senior Cycle SPHE guidance published (non-mandatory, guidelines only)

docs.title: 2.2 Junior Cycle Reform (2015–2023)
docs.text: Date Development 2015 Framework for Junior Cycle published – Wellbeing designated as a key pillar 2015–2017 Junior Cycle Wellbeing programme introduced, incorporating SPHE, CSPE, PE 2019 NCCA begins review of Junior Cycle SPHE specification 2022 New Junior Cycle SPHE specification approved September 2023 New Junior Cycle SPHE specification implemented for all first-year students

docs.title: 2.3 Senior Cycle Reform (2022–2027)
docs.text: Date Development 2022 Department of Education announces Senior Cycle reform programme 2023–2024 NCCA develops new Senior Cycle SPHE specification September 2024 New Senior Cycle SPHE specification published and available for voluntary adoption September 2025 Mandatory for Leaving Certificate Applied (LCA) students September 2027 Mandatory for all Senior Cycle students (Leaving Certificate Established)

docs.title: 2.4 Primary Curriculum Reform (2023–2026)
docs.text: Date Development 2023 Primary Curriculum Framework published by NCCA September 2025 New Wellbeing specification (integrating SPHE + PE) published; rollout begins 2025/26 2026–2027+ Phased enactment in schools (Wellbeing must be one of first three areas adopted)

docs.title: 3.1 Primary Legislation
docs.text: Act Relevance Education Act 1998 (as amended) Establishes NCCA; provides for curriculum development; sets out rights of parents and schools Education Welfare Act 2000 Compulsory education and attendance requirements Equal Status Acts 2000–2018 Non-discrimination in education; relevant to inclusive SPHE delivery Child and Family Agency Act 2013 Establishes TUSLA; child protection obligations relevant to SPHE teachers

docs.title: 3.2 Key Ministerial Circulars and Policy Documents
docs.text: Document Year Content Framework for Junior Cycle 2015 Wellbeing as key pillar; SPHE within Wellbeing programme Junior Cycle SPHE Specification 2023 Updated specification with 4 strands, 100 hours; mandatory from Sept 2023 Senior Cycle SPHE Specification 2024 New 3-strand specification; 60 hours; phased mandatory from 2025/2027 Primary Curriculum Framework 2023 Integrates SPHE and PE under "Wellbeing" curriculum area Wellbeing Policy Statement and Framework for Practice (2018–2023) 2018 DES/NCCA whole-school wellbeing framework for post-primary schools Senior Cycle Redevelopment 2022–ongoing Broader reform embedding wellbeing as key competency across all subjects

docs.title: 3.3 Official URLs
docs.text: Resource URL NCCA – Junior Cycle SPHE https://ncca.ie/en/junior-cycle/junior-cycle-subjects/sphe/ NCCA – Senior Cycle SPHE https://ncca.ie/en/senior-cycle/senior-cycle-subjects-and-short-courses/sphe/ Curriculum Online (specifications) https://www.curriculumonline.ie Department of Education – SPHE https://www.gov.ie/en/policy-information/e5b69-sphe/ Oide – SPHE support https://oide.ie/post-primary/home/wellbeing/sphe-junior-cycle/ Oide – SPHE Senior Cycle https://oide.ie/post-primary/home/wellbeing/sphe-senior-cycle/

docs.title: 4. SPHE within the Wider Wellbeing Framework
4.1 Junior Cycle Wellbeing Programme
docs.text:
SPHE at Junior Cycle is part of the broader Junior Cycle Wellbeing Programme, which requires: - 400 hours of Wellbeing across three years of Junior Cycle - Delivered through: SPHE, CSPE (Civic, Social and Political Education), PE, and additional components - Schools required to demonstrate a whole-school approach to wellbeing

Six Wellbeing Indicators that the programme aims to develop:

Indicator Description Active Leading a physically active life; engaged in learning Responsible Making healthy choices; taking responsibility for learning and actions Connected Feeling connected to school, community, and people Resilient Coping with challenges and setbacks Respected Feeling valued; respecting others Aware Being aware of own thoughts and feelings; understanding their impact

docs.title: 4.2 Senior Cycle Wellbeing as Key Competency
docs.text:
In the Senior Cycle reform, "Cultivating Wellbeing" is one of seven key competencies integrated across ALL revised subject specifications:

  1. Thinking and solving problems
  2. Being creative
  3. Communicating
  4. Working with others
  5. Participating in society
  6. Cultivating wellbeing ← SPHE central to this
  7. Managing learning and self

docs.title: 4.3 Parental Opt-Out Rights
docs.text: Under Irish law and education policy: - Parents retain the right to request a child be withdrawn from specific SPHE content that contravenes their moral or religious convictions - Once a student reaches age 18, they decide independently on their participation - This provision specifically applies to RSE (Relationships and Sexuality Education) content - Schools are required to inform parents of the SPHE programme content

docs.title: 5. Role of Key Institutions
docs.text: Institution Role in SPHE NCCA (National Council for Curriculum and Assessment) Develops and revises SPHE specifications; provides guidelines and support materials Department of Education Sets mandatory status, implementation timelines, policy Oide (Professional Development Service for Teachers) Delivers professional learning for SPHE teachers; prints CPD resources TUSLA (Child and Family Agency) Child protection framework relevant to mandatory reporting; links to SPHE safeguarding content HSE (Health Service Executive) Health promotion programmes supporting SPHE delivery; online resources FSAI / HIQA Food/health authority materials relevant to health-related SPHE content Schools Implement SPHE within own ethos and timetable

docs.title: DOCUMENT METADATA / METADANE DOKUMENTU
docs.text: Country / Kraj: Ireland / Irlandia Subject / Przedmiot: Social, Personal and Health Education (SPHE) Document type / Typ dokumentu: Curriculum specification – Junior Cycle / Podstawa programowa – Junior Cycle Education level / Poziom kształcenia: Post-primary, Junior Cycle (Years 1–3, ages 12–15) Year of implementation / Rok wdrożenia: September 2023 (mandatory for all 1st Year students) Publisher / Wydawca: National Council for Curriculum and Assessment (NCCA) Source / Źródło: https://ncca.ie/en/junior-cycle/junior-cycle-subjects/sphe/ ; https://www.curriculumonline.ie Retrieved / Data pobrania: 2025-04-04 Status: In force / Obowiązujący – September 2023

docs.title: 1.1 What is Junior Cycle SPHE?
docs.text: Social, Personal and Health Education (SPHE) is a mandatory subject at Junior Cycle in Irish post-primary schools (years 1–3, ages ~12–15). The updated specification, implemented from September 2023, replaces the previous 2000 SPHE specification.

docs.title: 1.2 Aims of the Subject
docs.text: The Junior Cycle SPHE specification aims to: - Build self-awareness and positive self-worth in students - Develop the knowledge, skills, and values necessary for students to lead fulfilling and healthy lives - Empower students to create and maintain respectful relationships with others - Enhance students' capacity to contribute positively to the world around them - Promote healthy decision-making and critical thinking about health-related topics - Provide a safe and supportive learning environment where students can explore personal and social issues

docs.title: 1.3 Key Structural Facts
docs.text: Feature Detail Total hours 100 hours over 3 years of Junior Cycle (up from 70 hours in previous spec) Year of introduction September 2023 (mandatory for incoming 1st Year students) Assessment Not formally examined at Junior Cycle Final Examination; assessed through classroom-based work Timetable Approximately 1 class per week (~70 min/week or equivalent) Delivery Typically by a dedicated SPHE teacher; whole-school approach also required Number of strands 4 main strands

docs.title: Strand 1: Understanding Myself and Others
docs.text:
This strand focuses on self-awareness, identity, and interpersonal understanding. Key themes include:

Year 1 (age ~12–13): - Exploring personal identity and individuality - Understanding emotions and emotional intelligence - Building self-esteem and positive self-concept - The importance of support networks: family, friends, community - Recognising strengths and areas for growth

Year 2 (age ~13–14): - How personal beliefs, values, and attitudes are shaped - Understanding stereotypes, bias, and prejudice - Building empathy and perspective-taking - Communication in relationships – verbal and non-verbal - Navigating peer pressure and social influence

Year 3 (age ~14–15): - Personal development and emerging adulthood - Exploring identity in a digital age - Understanding diversity and inclusion in Irish society - Civic identity and belonging to communities - Reflecting on personal growth over Junior Cycle

Representative learning outcomes: - Students should be able to identify and describe personal values and how they influence decisions - Students should be able to demonstrate empathy and active listening skills - Students should be able to reflect on how social media affects self-perception and identity

docs.title: Strand 2: Making Healthy Choices
docs.text:
This strand addresses physical health, lifestyle choices, substances, and health literacy. Key themes include:

Year 1 (age ~12–13): - Understanding what health means: physical, mental, emotional, social dimensions - Sleep, nutrition, and physical activity as foundations of health - Screen time and digital wellbeing – healthy habits online - Introduction to food, diet, and body image

Year 2 (age ~13–14): - Alcohol: facts, risks, societal attitudes; legal age and advertising - Tobacco and vaping (e-cigarettes): health risks, addiction and dependence - Drugs – including cannabis and new psychoactive substances (NPS/'headshop drugs') - How to refuse substances – refusal skills and assertiveness - Understanding addiction as a health issue

Year 3 (age ~14–15): - Effects of substances on the developing brain and long-term health - Gambling and gaming: understanding problematic behaviours - Access to health services in Ireland – where to get help - Critical evaluation of health information online and in media - First aid and emergency response awareness

Representative learning outcomes: - Students should be able to analyse advertising and peer influence on health-related choices - Students should be able to describe the short and long-term effects of alcohol and tobacco on the body - Students should be able to identify trusted sources of health information and support services

docs.title: Strand 3: Relationships and Sexuality
docs.text:
This strand takes a holistic, rights-based, and age-appropriate approach to relationships and sexuality. It builds progressively over the three years of Junior Cycle.

Year 1 (age ~12–13): - What makes a healthy relationship: respect, trust, communication, kindness - Friendships: forming, maintaining, and navigating difficulties - Puberty and physical development: understanding the changes - Personal boundaries – saying no; rights in relationships - Introduction to online relationships and digital communication safety

Year 2 (age ~13–14): - Understanding consent: what it means in friendships and relationships - Romantic relationships: feelings, expectations, pressure - Understanding gender: biological sex, gender identity, and social roles - Sexual orientation and diversity: respectful language and understanding - Healthy and unhealthy relationship behaviours; recognising early warning signs

Year 3 (age ~14–15): - Sexual health: understanding reproduction and contraception at an age-appropriate level - Sexually transmitted infections (STIs): key facts and prevention - Influence of pornography on attitudes, behaviours, and relationship expectations - Online grooming and exploitation: recognising and reporting - Developing healthy attitudes to sexuality as a part of human identity

Note: The Department of Education has explicitly stated that SPHE content is age-appropriate and evidence-based and does not include graphic or explicit material.

Representative learning outcomes: - Students should be able to explain what consent means and why it is central to healthy relationships - Students should be able to identify resources and supports for issues related to sexual health and relationships - Students should be able to critically evaluate the impact of pornography and media stereotypes on relationship expectations

docs.title: Strand 4: Emotional Wellbeing
docs.text:
This strand focuses on mental health, emotional literacy, and coping skills. Key themes include:

Year 1 (age ~12–13): - Understanding emotions: naming, expressing and regulating feelings - Stress and anxiety: recognising signs and constructive coping strategies - Importance of sleep and rest for emotional wellbeing - Building resilience: bouncing back from setbacks - School belonging and connection as protective factors

Year 2 (age ~13–14): - Mental health: what it is; challenging stigma - Understanding depression and anxiety: signs and symptoms - Self-harm and suicidal ideation: how to recognise and respond safely (safe messaging guidelines) - Seeking help: talking to trusted adults; professional support - Online wellbeing: social media, cyberbullying, and digital resilience

Year 3 (age ~14–15): - Positive psychology: strengths, gratitude, purpose, hope - Grief, loss, and bereavement: understanding and responding - Understanding eating difficulties and body image - Mindfulness and other evidence-based strategies for emotional regulation - Transition and change: moving from Junior to Senior Cycle

Key principle: SPHE adopts safe messaging guidelines when addressing topics such as suicide, self-harm, and mental health crisis – following guidance from the National Office for Suicide Prevention (NOSP) and HSE.

Representative learning outcomes: - Students should be able to demonstrate techniques to manage stress and anxiety - Students should be able to describe warning signs of a mental health difficulty in themselves or others and know how to seek help - Students should be able to explain how personal wellbeing can be protected and supported

docs.title: 3. Cross-Cutting Themes
docs.text:
Across all four strands, the specification embeds key cross-cutting themes:

Theme Application Digital literacy Evaluating online health information; online relationships; social media influence Equality and inclusion LGBTQ+ inclusion; diversity; disability awareness; anti-discrimination Human rights Rights in relationships; right to safety; right to health information Critical thinking Media literacy; advertising; misinformation Whole-school wellbeing SPHE connects to broader school wellbeing policy and culture

docs.title: 4. Learning Outcomes Framework
docs.text: The specification uses a learning outcomes model (consistent with broader Junior Cycle reform). Each learning outcome describes what the student should know, understand, and be able to do at the end of Junior Cycle.

docs.title: Sample Learning Outcomes by Strand
docs.text:
Strand 1 – Understanding Myself and Others:

"Appreciate how personal values and beliefs influence attitudes and behaviour"

"Examine how stereotypes and prejudice affect individuals and society"

Strand 2 – Making Healthy Choices:

"Explore the short and long-term effects of alcohol on a person's health and wellbeing"

"Demonstrate skills to make healthy choices in relation to physical and mental health"

Strand 3 – Relationships and Sexuality:

"Understand the concept of consent in the context of all relationships"

"Evaluate the influence of pornography on attitudes, expectations, and behaviours in relationships"

Strand 4 – Emotional Wellbeing:

"Identify strategies to cope with stress and emotional difficulties"

"Know where to seek help if they or someone they know is experiencing a mental health difficulty"

docs.title: 5. Assessment
docs.text: SPHE at Junior Cycle is not assessed through formal examinations. Assessment is: - Formative / classroom-based – ongoing feedback during learning - Focused on participation, reflection, and skills development - Schools may use well-designed tasks, discussions, creative projects, reflective journals - No Classroom-Based Assessment (CBA) requirement (unlike some other Junior Cycle subjects) - Recorded in the Junior Cycle Profile of Achievement (JCPA) as a subject completed

docs.title: 6.1 Teacher Requirements
docs.text:
SPHE is typically taught by a teacher with a background in: - Guidance Counselling - Home Economics - Physical Education - Biology / Science - Or any teacher who has completed SPHE professional development training

There is no single mandatory SPHE-specific qualification at Junior Cycle level; rather, professional development through Oide is expected.

docs.title: 6.2 Oide Professional Learning
docs.text:
Oide (the merged professional development service) provides: - Face-to-face workshops on implementing the new spec - Online courses and webinars - School cluster supports - Resources for SPHE planning and delivery

Resources available at: https://oide.ie/post-primary/home/wellbeing/sphe-junior-cycle/

docs.title: 7. Comparison with Previous (2000) Specification
docs.text: Feature Previous (2000) Spec New (2023) Spec Hours 70 hours over 3 years 100 hours over 3 years Strands 3 modules 4 strands RSE Separate RSE curriculum Integrated as Strand 3 Digital wellbeing Not explicitly included Explicit strand focus Emotional Wellbeing Limited coverage Dedicated Strand 4 Safe messaging Not formalised Embedded (NOSP guidelines) Learning outcomes model Objectives-based Learning outcomes model Mental health focus Basic Comprehensive

docs.title: 1.1 What is Senior Cycle SPHE?
docs.text: Social, Personal and Health Education (SPHE) at Senior Cycle is a mandatory, non-examined subject delivered in the final two years of secondary education (5th and 6th Year, ages ~15–18). The new specification, published in September 2024, replaces fragmented previous provision and creates for the first time a unified, consistent Senior Cycle SPHE curriculum for all students.

docs.title: 1.2 Why Was a New Specification Needed?
docs.text:
Prior to 2024, Senior Cycle SPHE provision was: - Inconsistent across schools – some provided it, many did not - Not specified in detail – only general guidelines existed (2006) - Delivered differently depending on school ethos, resources, and teacher availability - Disconnected from the more structured Junior Cycle provision

The reform responds to: - Evidence of poor mental health outcomes among Irish adolescents (HBSC 2022: nearly 50% of teens reporting low mood) - The wider Senior Cycle Redevelopment programme (2022 onwards) - Growing consensus about the need for consistent RSE (Relationships and Sexuality Education) provision at Senior Cycle - Demand from students, parents, teachers, and health professionals

docs.title: 1.3 Key Structural Facts
docs.text: Feature Detail Total hours 60 hours over 2 years of Senior Cycle (5th and 6th Year) Publication September 2024 Mandatory for LCA students September 2025 Mandatory for all Leaving Cert students September 2027 Examination Not examined in Leaving Certificate Number of strands 3 main strands Cross-cutting elements 3 elements threading through all strands Connection to LC reform Part of broader Senior Cycle Redevelopment; "Cultivating Wellbeing" is one of seven key competencies

docs.title: Strand 1: Health and Wellbeing
docs.text:
This strand helps students develop the knowledge, understanding, skills, and dispositions to support their physical, emotional, social, and spiritual wellbeing. It emphasises self-care, resilience, health literacy, and the ability to navigate health systems.

Key topics and learning areas:

Physical health: - Understanding the relationship between lifestyle choices and long-term health - Nutrition and healthy eating for adults – evidence-based guidance vs. diet culture myths - Physical activity: recommended levels, benefits for mental and physical health - Sexual and reproductive health: contraception, STIs, sexual health services - Preventive healthcare: screening, check-ups, vaccination as adult responsibility

Mental and emotional health: - Understanding mental health as a continuum, not a binary - Resilience and positive psychology: strengths, purpose, gratitude - Stress management strategies appropriate for students under exam pressure - Sleep and its critical role in cognitive function, mood, and health - Recognising and responding to anxiety, depression, eating disorders - Emotional regulation and self-compassion

Social health: - Social determinants of health: how socioeconomic factors affect wellbeing - Health inequalities in Ireland and globally - Community, belonging, and social connectedness as health factors - Volunteering and civic participation as wellbeing resources

Health literacy: - How to access, understand, and evaluate health information - Navigating the Irish health system (GP, Emergency Department, mental health services, HSE) - Rights and responsibilities as a health consumer - Critical evaluation of health claims in media, advertising, and online

Representative learning outcomes: - Students will be able to develop and implement a personal health plan addressing their own identified needs - Students will be able to describe the Irish health service landscape and identify appropriate pathways to care - Students will be able to critically evaluate health information from a range of sources - Students will be able to demonstrate strategies for building and maintaining positive mental health

docs.title: Strand 2: Relationships and Sexuality
docs.text:
This strand takes a holistic, rights-based approach to relationships and sexuality, building on the foundation established in Junior Cycle SPHE. It encourages students to develop healthy, respectful relationships both in-person and online, while understanding sexuality as a positive dimension of human identity.

Key topics and learning areas:

Consent and communication: - Understanding consent: active, ongoing, freely given, reversible, informed - Communication skills in intimate relationships: negotiating boundaries, expressing needs - The legal framework around consent in Ireland (Sexual Offences Act 2017) - Coercive control: recognising patterns of controlling behaviour in relationships - What to do if consent is violated: supports, reporting, legal rights

Relationships in the digital age: - Online relationships: safety, authenticity, respect - Sexting and digital intimacy: legal dimensions, peer pressure, consequence - Cyberbullying in the context of relationships: reporting and support - The role of pornography: influence on attitudes, expectations, and body image - Dating apps: responsible use; recognising predatory behaviour

Sexuality and identity: - Human sexuality as a spectrum: understanding sexual orientation and gender identity - LGBTQ+ identities: respectful language, inclusion, and Irish legal context - Fertility and reproductive health in young adults - Contraception: types, effectiveness, availability in Ireland - Sexually transmitted infections (STIs): prevention, testing, treatment - Pregnancy options in Ireland: up-to-date information including legal context post-2018

Relationships and violence: - Intimate partner violence: forms, impact, support services - Sexual violence and abuse: definitions, prevalence, responding and reporting - Safe relationships: recognising healthy vs. unhealthy dynamics in adulthood

Representative learning outcomes: - Students will be able to explain the concept of consent and apply it reflectively to varied relationship scenarios - Students will be able to identify signs of abusive relationships, including emotional, physical, sexual, and coercive control - Students will be able to describe the range of contraceptive methods available, their effectiveness, and where to access them in Ireland - Students will be able to demonstrate understanding of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities with respectful and inclusive language

docs.title: Strand 3: Into Adulthood
docs.text:
This strand focuses on preparing students for the transition to life beyond school – into higher education, the workforce, independent living, and adult citizenship. It nurtures life skills, self-advocacy, and the ability to navigate societal structures.

Key topics and learning areas:

Transitions and future pathways: - Post-school options: higher education (CAO system), further education, apprenticeships, employment - Managing change, uncertainty, and the stress of transition - Building a positive identity beyond academic results - Financial literacy: budgeting, managing money as a young adult, understanding debt and credit - Tenants' rights, accommodation options, homelessness awareness

Citizenship and society: - Democratic participation: voting, activism, community involvement - Understanding Irish and European political systems - Social justice and human rights: engaging with inequality - Climate change as a health and justice issue; individual and collective action - Media literacy and misinformation in a democratic society

Work and wellbeing: - Rights of workers in Ireland: employment law basics, contracts, trade unions - Managing work-life balance as a young adult - Recognising workplace stress, bullying, and harassment - The role of meaningful work in wellbeing and identity

Independent living: - Self-care in independent contexts (cooking, managing health appointments, exercise) - Mental health supports for young adults: accessing counselling, online tools, services - Alcohol and substance use in adult social contexts: informed decision-making - Building and maintaining supportive social networks in adulthood

Representative learning outcomes: - Students will be able to create a realistic personal financial plan for an early adult scenario - Students will be able to identify their roles and responsibilities as a citizen in a democratic society - Students will be able to locate and access appropriate supports for their own health and wellbeing needs post-school - Students will be able to evaluate the factors that contribute to a meaningful and healthy adult life

docs.title: 3. Cross-Cutting Elements
docs.text: Three cross-cutting elements thread through all three strands:

docs.title: Element 1: Thinking Critically and Empathetically
docs.text: Students are supported to: - Question assumptions and social norms - Consider multiple perspectives, including those of people with different identities and experiences - Apply ethical reasoning to health and social decisions - Develop empathy as a skill and disposition

docs.title: Element 2: Exercising Rights, Responsibilities, and Inclusivity
docs.text: Students are encouraged to: - Understand their rights in health, relationships, and civic life - Recognise corresponding responsibilities to self and others - Contribute to inclusive environments in school, online, and in society - Challenge discrimination and exclusion in any form

docs.title: Element 3: Being Health Literate
docs.text: Students develop the ability to: - Access and evaluate health information from multiple and varied sources - Navigate health and social services effectively - Communicate health needs clearly to professionals and others - Make evidence-informed decisions about their own health

docs.title: 4.1 Seven Key Competencies
docs.text:
The Senior Cycle Redevelopment programme defines seven key competencies to be developed across all subjects. SPHE is centrally aligned to "Cultivating Wellbeing" but also contributes to all others:

Competency SPHE Contribution Thinking and solving problems Critical evaluation of health information; ethical dilemmas Being creative Personal projects; creative approaches to wellbeing Communicating Assertiveness; consent conversations; advocacy Working with others Collaborative activities; peer support Participating in society Citizenship; volunteering; democratic engagement Cultivating wellbeing Core focus of SPHE across all 3 strands Managing learning and self Emotional regulation; self-advocacy; future planning

docs.title: 4.2 Connection to SPHE at Junior Cycle
docs.text: Senior Cycle SPHE builds upon the foundations of Junior Cycle SPHE (2023 spec), ensuring a coherent 5-year SPHE journey from 1st Year to 6th Year in post-primary school. Students build progressively on earlier knowledge and skills rather than repeating content.

docs.title: 5. Assessment
docs.text: Senior Cycle SPHE is not part of the Leaving Certificate examination. It is: - Non-examined – no terminal written exam - Reflected through classroom engagement and formative assessment - May include: projects, discussions, reflective journals, presentations - Does not contribute to Leaving Certificate points calculation - However, its mandatory status ensures it is tracked and reported by schools

docs.title: 6. Parental Opt-Out Provisions
docs.text: Consistent with the Education Act and Irish policy tradition: - Parents may request that their child be withdrawn from specific content that contravenes their religious or moral convictions - Students aged 18+ may decide independently about their own participation - Schools must inform parents of the content of the SPHE programme - Schools are encouraged to engage parents proactively and provide information note opportunities

docs.title: 7. Teacher Professional Development
docs.text:
Oide provides dedicated Senior Cycle SPHE professional learning, including: - Introductory workshops for teachers new to Senior Cycle SPHE - Deep-dive sessions on Strand 2 (Relationships & Sexuality) – most sensitive area - Online and in-school cluster support - Safe messaging training (for Strand 1 mental health content)

Resources: https://oide.ie/post-primary/home/wellbeing/sphe-senior-cycle/

docs.title: Ireland – SPHE: Implementation Context, FAQ and Comparative Analysis (2025)
1. Context of SPHE Reform in Ireland
1.1 Why Is SPHE Being Reformed Now?
docs.text:
Ireland is in the midst of a comprehensive curriculum reform at all levels of education. SPHE is being updated as part of this broader effort, but also in response to specific pressures:

Health pressures: - Adolescent mental health deterioration: HBSC 2022 found nearly 50% of Irish teenagers report low mood – more than doubling since 1998 - Rising rates of anxiety and depression among 12–18-year-olds - Increasing rates of overweight and obesity: ~17.7% of primary school-age children (2022–23) - Youth alcohol use, vaping, and cannabis experimentation remaining high - Significant gender gap in mental health outcomes – girls more affected than boys

Social and technological pressures: - Social media and smartphones creating new mental health challenges (FOMO, cyberbullying, body image) - Pornography increasingly accessible to under-18s, influencing relationship expectations - Online misinformation about health, bodies, and sexuality - Irish society becoming more diverse – SPHE must be inclusive of many backgrounds

Educational pressures: - Inconsistency of previous SPHE delivery (especially at Senior Cycle) – no guarantee students received any RSE or mental health education - Junior Cycle reform (2015) created the Wellbeing Programme, requiring more structured SPHE - Senior Cycle reform (2022) demanded a new mandatory SPHE specification - Post-COVID need to address gaps in student social-emotional learning

Legislative and policy drivers: - Health (Regulation of Termination of Pregnancy) Act 2018 – Ireland legalised abortion; SPHE required to provide up-to-date, accurate information about reproductive health options - Government's Healthy Ireland: A Framework for Improved Health and Wellbeing 2019–2025 - Department of Health's National Drugs Strategy 2017–2025 - Growing advocacy from student unions (USI, ISSU) for better RSE and mental health education

docs.title: 2.1 General Questions
docs.text:
Q: Is SPHE compulsory in Ireland? A: Yes. SPHE is mandatory at both Junior Cycle (3 years) and Senior Cycle (2 years). At Junior Cycle, the updated specification has been mandatory since September 2023. At Senior Cycle, the new 2024 specification is mandatory for LCA students from September 2025 and for all Leaving Cert students by September 2027.

Q: Does SPHE appear on the Leaving Certificate? A: No. Senior Cycle SPHE is not examined and does not contribute to CAO points. However, it is a mandatory curriculum component that schools must deliver and document.

Q: Is SPHE the same as sex education? A: SPHE is broader than sex education. RSE (Relationships and Sexuality Education) is one strand of SPHE (Strand 3 at Junior Cycle; Strand 2 at Senior Cycle). SPHE also covers mental health, making healthy lifestyle choices, substance use, civic preparation, and transition to adulthood.

Q: Can parents withdraw their child from SPHE? A: Parents may request withdrawal from specific content that contravenes their moral or religious convictions – this applies specifically to content touching on sexuality and reproduction. They cannot withdraw a child from SPHE entirely. When students reach age 18, they decide independently.

Q: How many hours per year does SPHE take? A: Junior Cycle: approximately 33 hours per year (100 hours over 3 years). Senior Cycle: approximately 30 hours per year (60 hours over 2 years).

docs.title: 2.2 Content-Related Questions
docs.text:
Q: Does SPHE cover mental health? A: Yes, comprehensively. Strand 4 (Emotional Wellbeing) at Junior Cycle covers: emotional literacy, stress management, depression, self-harm (safe messaging), crisis response, resilience, and seeking help from services. Senior Cycle Strand 1 (Health and Wellbeing) deepens this with evidence-based coping strategies, mental health service navigation, and adult transitions.

Q: Does SPHE cover LGBTQ+ topics? A: Yes. Both Junior and Senior Cycle specifications include LGBTQ+ identities explicitly. This includes understanding sexual orientation, gender identity, respectful language, and the legal context (Ireland has recognised same-sex marriage since 2015 and gender recognition since 2015). Organisations like BeLonG To provide school resources.

Q: Does SPHE address addiction and substance use? A: Yes. At Junior Cycle, alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, and other substances are covered in Strand 2 (Making Healthy Choices) including effects on the developing brain. At Senior Cycle, students revisit substance use in the broader context of adult decision-making and health literacy.

Q: Is pornography discussed in SPHE? A: Yes. The 2023 Junior Cycle specification explicitly includes the influence of pornography on attitudes, behaviours, and relationship expectations as a learning outcome within the Relationships and Sexuality strand. This was a deliberate, research-informed addition to address a growing issue affecting Irish young people.

Q: Does Senior Cycle SPHE address the topic of abortion? A: Yes. Since Ireland changed its law in 2018, SPHE is expected to provide factually accurate and non-judgemental information about pregnancy options available in Ireland, including access to termination services. This is part of reproductive health content in Strand 2.

Q: Is One Health or environmental health part of SPHE? A: Not explicitly as a dedicated area – unlike the Polish model (Edukacja Zdrowotna Dział VIII). However, Strand 3 (Into Adulthood) at Senior Cycle touches on climate change as a health and justice issue, and health literacy broadly includes environmental health awareness. This is less developed than in the Polish curriculum.

docs.title: 2.3 Teacher and School Questions
docs.text:
Q: Who delivers SPHE? A: Any qualified teacher can deliver SPHE. In practice, it is most commonly taught by Guidance Counsellors, Home Economics teachers, PE teachers, or Biology teachers. Unlike in Poland, there is no single mandatory qualification pathway for SPHE teachers.

Q: Does every school have an SPHE teacher? A: The Department of Education requires all post-primary schools to provide SPHE. However, the reality varies – not all schools have a dedicated SPHE teacher, and provision can vary significantly depending on school ethos, resources, and principal leadership.

Q: What training supports SPHE teachers? A: Oide (the national teacher professional development service) is the primary support. They provide workshops, online resources, cluster support, and specialist materials. Completion of training is not mandatory but strongly encouraged.

Q: Can a school choose not to teach SPHE? A: No – SPHE is mandatory. However, schools have autonomy over how they timetable and deliver it, and oversight is primarily through school self-evaluation (SSE) rather than inspections focused solely on SPHE.

4.1 Structural Comparison
docs.text: Feature Ireland (SPHE) Poland (Edukacja Zdrowotna) Subject name Social, Personal and Health Education Edukacja Zdrowotna First introduced (post-primary) 2000 (Junior Cycle) 2025 Current key specification year 2023 (JC) / 2024 (SC) 2025 Mandatory? Yes (JC + SC) Yes Total hours (post-primary) 160 hours (100 JC + 60 SC) ~120–140 hours total Is it examined? No (neither JC nor SC) No (no Leaving Cert equivalent) Number of thematic areas 4 strands (JC) / 3 strands (SC) 11 areas (one curriculum) Oversight body NCCA MEN + ORE Teacher support body Oide ORE + ZPE Digital resources Spunout, HSE website, Oide resources ZPE (dedicated digital platform)

docs.title: 4.2 Thematic Coverage Comparison
docs.text: Health Theme Ireland SPHE Poland EZ Mental health / Emotional wellbeing ✅ Dedicated strand (JC Strand 4; SC Strand 1) ✅ Dział V Relationships and sexuality ✅ Dedicated strand (JC Strand 3; SC Strand 2) ✅ Dział VII Physical health / Healthy choices ✅ JC Strand 2 ✅ Dział II Nutrition and diet ✅ Within JC Strand 2 ✅ Dedicated Dział IV Physical activity ✅ PE separate (400h Wellbeing programme) ✅ Dedicated Dział III Substance use and addiction ✅ JC Strand 2 ✅ Dedicated Dział IX Social health and relationships ✅ All strands ✅ Dział VI Environmental / Planetary health ⚠️ Partial (SC Strand 3 only) ✅ Dedicated Dział VIII (incl. One Health) Health system literacy ✅ SC Strand 1 ✅ Dedicated Dział X Citizenship / Into adulthood ✅ Dedicated (SC Strand 3) ⚠️ No dedicated dział; embedded Digital health / Media literacy ✅ Cross-cutting theme ✅ Included in Dział IX Values and attitudes ✅ Embedded throughout ✅ Dedicated Dział I Dojrzewanie / Puberty ✅ JC Strand 3 (Year 1) ✅ Only at primary (not post-primary)

docs.title: 4.3 Key Similarities
docs.text:
1. Both are mandatory at post-primary level
  2. Both are non-examined – no high-stakes assessment
  3. Both adopt holistic definitions of health (bio-psycho-social models)
  4. Both emphasise active, participatory learning methods
  5. Both include RSE/sexuality education as a core component
  6. Both require whole-school wellbeing approaches
  7. Both use national bodies for curriculum development and teacher support (NCCA/ORE)

docs.title: 4.4 Key Differences
docs.text: Aspect Ireland Poland Longevity 25 years of SPHE provision (since 1999/2000) Brand new from 2025 Environmental health Limited; Poland has stronger One Health framing One Health (Planetary Health) as explicit dział Opt-out rights Parents have right to opt out of specific RSE content No opt-out – fully mandatory Digital platform Various partner sites (no single ZPE-equivalent) Dedicated ZPE platform with all materials Teacher qualifications No single required pathway; any teacher+CPD Defined pathway (biology/WF + postgraduate diploma in EZ) Citizenship strand Explicit (SC Strand 3: Into Adulthood, + CSPE) Less explicit; embedded in social health dział Interconnection with health system Strong (SC Strand 1: navigating Irish HSE) Strong (Dział X: system ochrony zdrowia)

docs.title: 4.5 Irish Good Practices Worth Considering for Polish EZ
docs.text:
1. Spiral curriculum design across 5+ years of post-primary – Poland could deepen 11-dział structure progressively across all 4 years of liceum
  2. Explicit "Into Adulthood" strand – preparing students for independent adult life (financial literacy, tenants' rights, job rights) not yet prominent in Polish EZ
  3. 400-hour Junior Cycle Wellbeing Programme – embedding wellbeing across SPHE + CSPE + PE in an interconnected way
  4. Safe messaging formalisation – Ireland's mandatory safe messaging for suicide/self-harm content is a model for Poland
  5. Dedicated organisations (Spunout, BeLonG To, Jigsaw) providing independent, student-facing resources that complement classroom SPHE
  6. Parental opt-out procedure – Ireland's structured, limited opt-out framework may be a useful model for navigating Polish parental concerns

docs.title: 4.6 Polish EZ Good Practices Worth Considering for Irish SPHE
docs.text:
1. One Health / Planetary Health as an explicit area (Dział VIII) – stronger than Ireland's approach
  2. Dedicated ZPE digital platform – centralised, nationally consistent digital resources for all schools
  3. Mandatory teacher qualification pathway – more rigorous and standardised than Ireland's
  4. Dedicated Nutrition dział – Ireland covers nutrition within broader "Making Healthy Choices" but less systematically
  5. System ochrony zdrowia (health system literacy) – Poland's Dział X is comprehensive; Ireland covers it partially in SC Strand 1

docs.title: 5.1 Healthy Ireland Framework (2019–2025)
docs.text:
SPHE sits within Ireland's national health promotion strategy: - Goal: "A healthier Ireland with wellbeing at its centre" - Builds on original Healthy Ireland Framework (2013) - Identifies schools as key settings for health promotion - SPHE is a core delivery mechanism for school-based health promotion

Key pillars relevant to SPHE: 1. Healthy eating and active living 2. Mental health and wellbeing 3. Tobacco, alcohol, and drug reduction 4. Sexual health and crisis pregnancy prevention

Link: https://www.gov.ie/en/publication/healthy-ireland/

docs.title: 5.2 National Drugs Strategy (2017–2025)
docs.text: Ireland's drug strategy (Reducing Harm, Supporting Recovery) explicitly identifies schools and SPHE as key prevention settings. SPHE substance use content must align with: - Evidence-based harm reduction messaging - Age-appropriate information - Signposting to support services (HSE Drugs helpline: 1800 459 459)

docs.title: Ireland – SPHE Methodology, Wellbeing Framework and Teacher Support (2023–2025)
1.1 Guiding Principles
docs.text:
The Irish SPHE curriculum is built on a set of core pedagogical principles that distinguish it from more traditional, content-heavy subjects:

1. Student-Centred Learning SPHE places the student's own experiences, questions, and needs at the centre of learning. The curriculum deliberately moves away from purely teacher-led instruction toward facilitated discussion, inquiry, and reflection.

2. Spiral Curriculum Design Themes introduced at primary level re-emerge and deepen at Junior Cycle, then again at Senior Cycle. Students revisit core concepts (e.g., consent, mental health, healthy choices) with increasing complexity and sophistication at each stage.

3. Holistic Understanding of Health Following the WHO definition, Irish SPHE treats health as encompassing: - Physical wellbeing - Mental and emotional wellbeing - Social wellbeing - Spiritual/existential wellbeing (in age-appropriate ways)

4. Rights-Based Approach The curriculum is grounded in children's and human rights frameworks. Students learn about their rights in relationships, in healthcare settings, as citizens, and in digital spaces.

5. Evidence-Based Practice Content is developed in line with: - WHO guidance on health education - NCCA research on adolescent development - HBSC (Health Behaviour in School-aged Children) Ireland data - National clinical guidelines (HSE, NOSP)

6. Safe Learning Environment Given the sensitivity of many SPHE topics, the curriculum explicitly requires teachers to: - Establish ground rules at the outset (group agreement/contract) - Create psychological safety so students can engage honestly - Use distancing techniques – discussing issues in third person or through scenarios to avoid personal disclosure pressure - Follow safe messaging guidelines (for suicide, self-harm, eating disorders)

docs.title: 2.1 Active and Participatory Learning
docs.text:
NCCA and Oide recommend moving beyond lecture formats to active learning approaches:

Method Description Suitable for... Discussion circles Structured group discussions with ground rules Exploring values, relationships, emotional topics Case studies / scenarios Analysis of realistic situations (names changed, fictionalised) Consent, substance use, peer pressure situations Role play and simulation Acting out situations and practising responses Refusal skills, communication, consent Debate and structured controversy Exploring two sides of health/social issues systematically Advertising, alcohol policy, social media Reflective journaling Private writing about personal responses and insights Emotional wellbeing, identity, values Gallery walks Moving around classroom stations with prompts and posters Generating discussion on multiple topics simultaneously Fishbowl discussion Small group discusses while others observe then swap Deep discussion on sensitive topics Think-Pair-Share Individual reflection, partner discussion, group sharing Warm-up to sensitive topics; reducing anxiety Project-based learning Students research and create outputs (videos, campaigns) Health promotion; citizenship strand Guest speakers Professionals (psychologist, nurse, youth worker) sharing expertise Credibility; reducing stigma

docs.title: 2.2 Distancing Techniques (Critical for Sensitive Topics)
docs.text: When dealing with topics like mental health, sexual health, or substance use, teachers are trained to: - Use anonymised case studies rather than asking for personal disclosures - Frame discussion as: "What might someone your age be thinking/feeling in this situation?" - Use art, music, film, literature as indirect entry points to personal topics - Deploy question boxes – anonymous written questions students can submit

docs.title: 2.3 Technology and Digital Tools
docs.text: Recommended digital tools for SPHE delivery: - HSE.ie resources – interactive health content for students - Childline online resources – for mental health strand - Spunout.ie – peer-written mental health content for Irish young people - BeLonG To resources – LGBTQ+ inclusive content - NCCA Curriculum Online – lesson ideas and planning guides - Jigsaw.ie – whole-school mental health programme resources

docs.title: 3.1 Overview
docs.text:
The Junior Cycle Wellbeing Programme is a mandatory whole-school programme (not just one subject) that frames SPHE within a broader context of student flourishing.

Time allocation: 400 hours of Wellbeing across three years of Junior Cycle

This 400 hours is delivered through: - SPHE – 100 hours (updated specification 2023) - CSPE (Civic, Social and Political Education) – 100 hours - Physical Education (PE) – 100 hours - Additional Wellbeing provision – 100 hours (school-designed: e.g., mindfulness, yoga, career guidance sessions, Transition Year preparation, etc.)

docs.title: 3.2 Six Wellbeing Indicators
docs.text:
The programme is structured around developing six wellbeing indicators in students:

Indicator What it looks like in practice Active Students are physically engaged; participate willingly in school activities and learning Responsible Students make thoughtful decisions; show accountability for their choices Connected Students feel they belong to the school community and have meaningful relationships Resilient Students can bounce back from adversity; they have coping strategies and supports Respected Students feel heard and valued by peers, teachers, and staff; they respect others Aware Students have self-awareness about their thoughts, feelings, and impact on others

docs.title: 3.3 Whole-School Wellbeing Approach
docs.text: SPHE is most effective when embedded in a whole-school culture of wellbeing. This means: - Wellbeing is everyone's responsibility – not just the SPHE teacher - School leadership models positive wellbeing (staff wellbeing matters too) - Physical environment supports wellbeing (access to green space, quiet areas, safe corridors) - Anti-bullying policies (Bí Cineálta guidelines) are actively implemented - School uses School Self-Evaluation (SSE) to assess and improve wellbeing outcomes - Parents are engaged as partners in supporting student wellbeing

docs.title: 4. Senior Cycle Wellbeing – Cultivating Wellbeing as a Key Competency
4.1 Embedding Wellbeing Across the Senior Cycle
docs.text:
In the Senior Cycle Redevelopment (2022 onwards), "Cultivating Wellbeing" is one of seven key competencies expected of all Senior Cycle students, across all subjects. This means:

  • Teachers of ALL subjects are expected to be mindful of student wellbeing
  • Subject specifications include explicit competency descriptors
  • SPHE is the primary subject for this competency but it is not SPHE's exclusive domain

"Cultivating Wellbeing" competency descriptors for Senior Cycle students:

"Students develop self-awareness and self-management; they practise self-care and look after their physical and mental health; they show empathy and care for others; they reflect on their values and aspirations and manage stress effectively."

docs.title: 4.2 SPHE's Unique Role
docs.text: While wellbeing is whole-school, SPHE provides: - The dedicated space for explicit discussions about health, relationships, and personal development - 60 structured hours for students to develop knowledge and skills they may not encounter elsewhere - A structured relationship between teacher and class group in a non-examination context - Opportunity for students to develop health literacy in a focused, deliberate way

docs.title: 5.1 Principles of SPHE Assessment
docs.text: SPHE assessment is fundamentally formative and process-oriented: - The goal is to support student learning and growth, not to rank or grade - No terminal written examination at either Junior or Senior Cycle - Teachers use assessment to inform their teaching, not solely to report on students

docs.title: 5.2 Examples of Assessment Methods Used
docs.text: Method Description Reflective journal Students record personal responses, learning, and insights over the year Portfolio Collection of work demonstrating engagement and growth Discussion contributions Quality of participation in group discussions Case study analysis Written or oral analysis of a health or social scenario Personal health project Independent or group research project on a chosen health topic Peer assessment Students give constructive feedback to each other on projects Self-assessment Students rate their own learning and identify areas of development

docs.title: 5.3 What Is Avoided in SPHE Assessment
docs.text:
• Assessing personal beliefs or values (these are not assessable)
  • Grading emotional responses or degree of personal disclosure
  • Ranking students against each other
  • High-stakes memory testing of factual content
  • Assessing lifestyle choices outside the school setting

docs.title: 6.1 Who Teaches SPHE?
docs.text: SPHE may be taught by any qualified teacher, but strong practice is supported by teachers with backgrounds in: - Guidance Counselling – experience in personal development work - Home Economics – health and nutrition expertise - Physical Education – wellbeing and body awareness background - Biology – knowledge of human health and reproduction - Religious Education – experience with values and ethical questions (though SPHE is secular)

docs.title: 6.2 Role of Oide (Professional Development Service)
docs.text:
Oide is the merged professional development service for Irish teachers (formed 2022 from PDST, JCT and others). For SPHE, Oide provides:

For Junior Cycle SPHE: - National rollout workshops for teachers on the 2023 specification - Strand-specific resources and lesson exemplars - Support for school cluster groups - Guidance on safe messaging when discussing sensitive topics

For Senior Cycle SPHE: - Introductory workshops on the new 2024 specification - Deep-dive CPD on Strand 2 (Relationships and Sexuality) – most complex area - Online modules accessible at any time - School visit support for SPHE coordinators

Oide SPHE resources: https://oide.ie/post-primary/home/wellbeing/

docs.title: 6.3 Safe Messaging Training
docs.text: All SPHE teachers are encouraged to complete training in: - Safe messaging on suicide and self-harm – following HSE/NOSP guidelines - Child protection procedures – mandatory for all teachers (Tusla reporting obligations) - Inclusive SPHE delivery – particularly for LGBTQ+ content (BeLonG To training)

docs.title: 🇮🇪 Ireland (IE) — Document Registry
docs.text:
Health Education System: Social, Personal and Health Education (SPHE) Bioregion: Atlantic / Island Reform Status: Ongoing reform (Junior Cycle 2023, Senior Cycle 2024, Primary 2025)

This registry lists all source documents identified for Ireland in the OneHealth EU project. Documents are grouped by category. Each entry includes: a short description, document type, year, and a link to the download page or direct URL.

docs.title: System Overview
docs.text: Ireland has one of the most developed health education systems in the EU. The subject SPHE (Social, Personal and Health Education) is mandatory at all levels: Primary, Junior Cycle (post-primary, Years 1–3), and Senior Cycle (post-primary, Years 5–6). The system is grounded in a holistic understanding of health (physical, mental, social, spiritual) and a rights-based approach. Reforms undertaken between 2022 and 2025 significantly expanded the scope and contact hours of SPHE.

docs.title: 1. Education Act 1998 (as amended)
docs.text:
• Type: Primary legislation
  • Year: 1998 (with subsequent amendments)
  • Publisher: Oireachtas (Irish Parliament)
  • Description: The foundational statute governing the Irish education system. Establishes the NCCA (National Council for Curriculum and Assessment), defines the rights of parents and schools, including the parental right to opt out of SPHE content that conflicts with their moral or religious convictions. Provides the legal basis for curriculum development.
  • Access page: https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/1998/act/51/enacted/en/html

docs.title: 2. Education Welfare Act 2000
docs.text:
• Type: Primary legislation
  • Year: 2000
  • Publisher: Oireachtas
  • Description: Regulates compulsory schooling and attendance (ages 6–16). Provides the legal context for the mandatory status of SPHE and related wellbeing programmes.
  • Access page: https://www.irishstatutebook.ie/eli/2000/act/22/enacted/en/html

docs.title: 3. Junior Cycle SPHE Specification (2023)
docs.text:
• Type: Curriculum specification
  • Year: 2023 (mandatory implementation from September 2023)
  • Publisher: National Council for Curriculum and Assessment (NCCA) / curriculumonline.ie
  • Level: Post-primary, Junior Cycle (Years 1–3, ages 12–15)
  • Description: The updated SPHE specification for Junior Cycle, replacing the previous 2000 specification. Expanded to 100 hours across 3 years (up from 70 hours). Structured around four strands: (1) Understanding Myself and Others, (2) Making Healthy Choices, (3) Relationships and Sexuality, (4) Emotional Wellbeing. RSE (Relationships and Sexuality Education) is fully integrated as Strand 3. No terminal examination — assessment is formative and classroom-based.
  • Specification page (NCCA): https://ncca.ie/en/junior-cycle/junior-cycle-subjects/sphe/
  • Curriculum Online (specification + materials): https://www.curriculumonline.ie/junior-cycle/junior-cycle-subjects/sphe/

docs.title: 4. Senior Cycle SPHE Specification (2024)
docs.text:
• Type: Curriculum specification
  • Year: Published September 2024; mandatory for LCA: September 2025; mandatory for Leaving Cert Established: September 2027
  • Publisher: NCCA / curriculumonline.ie
  • Level: Post-primary, Senior Cycle (Years 5–6, ages 15–18)
  • Description: The first unified and comprehensive SPHE specification for Senior Cycle — prior to 2024, no consistent programme existed at this level. 60 hours across 2 years. Three strands: (1) Health and Wellbeing, (2) Relationships and Sexuality, (3) Into Adulthood. Three cross-cutting elements: thinking critically and empathetically, exercising rights and responsibilities, being health literate. Not examined in the Leaving Certificate.
  • Specification page (NCCA): https://ncca.ie/en/senior-cycle/senior-cycle-subjects-and-short-courses/sphe/
  • Curriculum Online: https://www.curriculumonline.ie/senior-cycle/senior-cycle-subjects/sphe/

docs.title: 5. Primary Curriculum Framework (2023)
docs.text:
• Type: Curriculum framework
  • Year: 2023 (published); phased rollout from 2025/26
  • Publisher: NCCA
  • Level: Primary (Junior Infants – 6th Class, ages 4–12)
  • Description: The new overarching curriculum framework for primary schools. SPHE and Physical Education (PE) are merged into a single Wellbeing curriculum area. Schools are required to adopt Wellbeing as one of the first three curriculum areas to implement in the rollout phase (from 2025/26).
  • Access page: https://ncca.ie/en/primary/primary-curriculum-framework/

docs.title: 6. Framework for Junior Cycle 2015
docs.text:
• Type: Policy framework / Curriculum framework
  • Year: 2015
  • Publisher: Department of Education Ireland (DES)
  • Description: The Junior Cycle reform document that established Wellbeing as one of four key pillars of Junior Cycle education. Introduced the Wellbeing Programme (400 hours across 3 years), delivered through SPHE (100h), CSPE (100h), PE (100h), and additional school-designed wellbeing components (100h). The foundational document for the current shape of SPHE at Junior Cycle.
  • Access page + PDF: https://www.gov.ie/en/publication/83d7a-framework-for-junior-cycle-2015/
  • Direct PDF: https://assets.gov.ie/24999/ded3c3db879a421c86dca19de69eb7ee.pdf

docs.title: 7. Wellbeing Policy Statement and Framework for Practice 2018–2023
docs.text:
• Type: Policy document
  • Year: 2018
  • Publisher: Department of Education and Skills (DES)
  • Level: Post-primary
  • Description: The comprehensive wellbeing policy for post-primary schools. Defines six student wellbeing indicators (Active, Responsible, Connected, Resilient, Respected, Aware). Establishes the whole-school approach to wellbeing across four domains: Culture and Environment, Curriculum, Relationships and Partnerships, Policy and Planning. Directly informs the SPHE programme and its broader school context.
  • Direct PDF: https://assets.gov.ie/25111/35c956d4d15a41e4a82ccd36ce37db4b.pdf
  • Access page: https://www.gov.ie/en/publication/wellbeing-policy-statement-and-framework-for-practice/

docs.title: 8. RSE Guidance for Schools (2023 update)
docs.text:
• Type: Guidance document
  • Year: 2023
  • Publisher: Department of Education Ireland
  • Description: Updated guidance for schools on delivering RSE (Relationships and Sexuality Education) as an integral component of SPHE. Addresses parental opt-out rights, the ethos dimension, age-appropriate content frameworks, and safe messaging requirements. Key document for understanding the public debate around SPHE in Ireland.
  • Access page (SPHE/RSE): https://www.gov.ie/en/policy-information/e5b69-sphe/

docs.title: 9. Junior Cycle Wellbeing Guidelines (NCCA, 2017)
docs.text:
• Type: Guidelines
  • Year: 2017
  • Publisher: NCCA
  • Description: NCCA guidance for implementing the Wellbeing Programme at Junior Cycle. Describes the structure of the 400-hour Wellbeing Programme, the role of SPHE, CSPE and PE within it, and practical guidance for schools on timetabling and school self-evaluation (SSE) for wellbeing.
  • Access page: https://ncca.ie/en/junior-cycle/wellbeing/

docs.title: 10. Senior Cycle Redevelopment — Overview and Reform Documents (2022–ongoing)
docs.text:
• Type: Policy reform documents
  • Year: 2022 (announced); ongoing implementation
  • Publisher: Department of Education Ireland
  • Description: A suite of documents underpinning the broader Senior Cycle reform programme. Defines seven key competencies for Senior Cycle, including Cultivating Wellbeing (the competency central to SPHE). Provides the policy rationale for making Senior Cycle SPHE mandatory from 2025/2027.
  • Access page: https://www.gov.ie/en/policy-information/senior-cycle/

docs.title: 11. Oide SPHE — Junior Cycle Teacher Resources
docs.text:
• Type: Teacher support / Professional development resources
  • Year: 2023 – present
  • Publisher: Oide (Professional Development Service for Teachers)
  • Description: Online platform providing professional support for teachers delivering Junior Cycle SPHE. Includes lesson plans, strand-specific materials, exemplar tasks, safe messaging guidance, online courses, and cluster group support. Oide was formed in 2022 from the merger of PDST, JCT and other services.
  • Access page: https://oide.ie/post-primary/home/wellbeing/sphe-junior-cycle/

docs.title: 12. Oide SPHE — Senior Cycle Teacher Resources
docs.text:
• Type: Teacher support / Professional development resources
  • Year: 2024 – present
  • Publisher: Oide
  • Description: Support materials for teachers implementing the new 2024 Senior Cycle SPHE specification. Particular focus on Strand 2 (Relationships and Sexuality) as the most complex delivery area. Includes online modules, introductory workshops, and in-school cluster visit support.
  • Access page: https://oide.ie/post-primary/home/wellbeing/sphe-senior-cycle/

docs.title: 13. HBSC Ireland 2022 — Health Behaviour in School-aged Children
docs.text:
• Type: Research report
  • Year: 2022
  • Publisher: University of Galway (in partnership with WHO)
  • Description: The Irish edition of the international HBSC study. A key empirical document — findings (including that nearly 50% of Irish teenagers report low mood) provided a direct evidence base for the 2024 Senior Cycle SPHE reform. Covers health, wellbeing, risk behaviours, and the social environment of children and young people in Ireland. New topics in the 2022 edition include loneliness, menstrual health, and the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic. A Trends Report (1998–2022) is also available.
  • Access page + downloads: https://www.universityofgalway.ie/hbsc/

docs.title: F. Supporting Organisations and Public Health Resources
14. HSE — Healthy Ireland Framework 2019–2025
docs.text:
• Type: National health strategy
  • Year: 2019 (updated 2024)
  • Publisher: Department of Health Ireland / Health Service Executive (HSE)
  • Description: The national public health strategy to which SPHE directly refers. Defines public health priorities (mental health, physical activity, addiction prevention) that align with SPHE programme goals at school level.
  • Access page (HSE): https://www.hse.ie/eng/about/who/healthyireland/

docs.title: 15. Safe Messaging Guidelines — Suicide and Self-Harm (HSE / NOSP, 2022)
docs.text:
• Type: Clinical guidelines
  • Year: 2022
  • Publisher: HSE / National Office for Suicide Prevention (NOSP)
  • Description: Safe messaging guidelines for communicating about suicide and self-harm. Embedded in both the Junior Cycle (Strand 4: Emotional Wellbeing) and Senior Cycle SPHE specifications — SPHE teachers are required to follow these guidelines. A mandatory reference for schools addressing mental health topics.
  • Access page: https://www.nosp.ie/resources/safe-messaging/

docs.title: G. Analytical Files in Project Repository (NotebookLM)
docs.text:
The following analytical documents were prepared for this project, based on the sources listed above:

File Contents IE_SPHE_Akt_Prawny_Kontekst_Legislacyjny.md Legal and historical context of SPHE — from 1999 to 2025; key acts, policies, reform timeline IE_SPHE_Curriculum_Junior_Cycle_2023.md Full analysis of the Junior Cycle 2023 specification — 4 strands, learning outcomes, assessment, comparison with the 2000 programme IE_SPHE_Curriculum_Senior_Cycle_2024.md Full analysis of the Senior Cycle 2024 specification — 3 strands, cross-cutting elements, connection to the Senior Cycle Redevelopment IE_SPHE_Metodyka_Wellbeing_Framework.md SPHE teaching methodology, Junior Cycle Wellbeing Programme (400h), 6 wellbeing indicators, supporting organisations IE_SPHE_FAQ_Kontekst_Porownanie_PL_2025.md FAQ and comparison of Irish SPHE with Polish health education (context for the OneHealth EU project)

docs.title: Repubblica Italiana – Curriculum, HBSC 2022 i One Health
1.1 Educazione Civica (Przedmiot Poprzeczny)
docs.text:
• Benessere psicofisico: Zdrowie psychiczne, asertywność, radzenie sobie ze stresem.
  • Educazione alimentare: Dieta śródziemnomorska (Dieta Mediterranea) jako dziedzictwo i standard zdrowia.
  • Dipendenze: Profilaktyka alkoholu, tytoniu i nowych narkotyków.
  • Cyberbullismo: Bezpieczeństwo w sieci i higiena cyfrowa.

docs.title: 1.2 Scienze (Nauki Przyrodnicze)
docs.text:
• Biologia umana: Budowa ciała, układ odpornościowy, szczepienia.
  • Riproduzione: Biologiczne podstawy, zmiany hormonalne.
  • Ecology & One Health: Powiązania między zdrowiem człowieka a stanem środowiska (szczególnie w kontekście zmian klimatu w basenie Morza Śródziemnego).

docs.title: 1.3 Scienze Motorie e Sportive (WF)
docs.text:
• Aktywność fizyczna jako prewencja chorób cywilizacyjnych.
  • Znaczenie sportu dla integracji społecznej.

docs.title: 2. Statystyki Zdrowia – HBSC Italia 2022
docs.text: Badanie koordynowane przez Istituto Superiore di Sanità (ISS) na próbie uczniów w wieku 11, 13, 15 i 17 lat.

docs.title: 2.1 Zdrowie Psychiczne i dobrostan
docs.text: Wskaźnik IT 2022 Uwaga Negatywny wpływ pandemii na psychikę 41% Bardzo wysoki subiektywny odczucie pogorszenia. Objawy psychosomatyczne (tygodniowo) ↑ wzrost vs 2018 Dominują bóle głowy, brzucha i drażliwość. Różnica płci Dziewczęta >> Chłopcy Znacznie gorsze samopoczucie u dziewcząt 15-17 lat. Satysfakcja z życia ↓ spadek Ogólny trend spadkowy w pokoleniu post-pandemicznym.

docs.title: 2.2 Otyłość i Żywienie
docs.text: Wskaźnik IT 2022 Komentarz Nadwaga i otyłość ↑ wzrost Włochy mają jeden z wyższych wskaźników otyłości dziecięcej w UE. Śniadania ↓ spadek Częste omijanie śniadań (szczególnie przez dziewczęta). Aktywność fizyczna (60 min/dz) <10% (🚨) Krytycznie niska aktywność; Włosi są jednymi z najbardziej biernych ruchowo nastolatków w UE.

docs.title: 2.3 Substancje i Zachowania Ryzykowne
docs.text: Substancja IT 2022 Trend Alkohol (użytkowanie bieżące) ~40% Wysoka akceptacja kulturowa "picia do posiłku". Fumo (palenie tytoniu) ~20% Wyższy odsetek palących dziewcząt niż chłopców. Cannabis (ost. 30 dni) ~11% Stabilny, ale wysoki poziom. Gioco d'azzardo (Hazard) 40% (17-latkowie) 🚨 Poważny problem społeczny; 57% chłopców w wieku 17 lat grało w hazard.

docs.title: 3. One Health / Planetary Health we Włoszech
3.1 Kontekst Instytucjonalny
docs.text: ISS (Istituto Superiore di Sanità) promuje podejście One Health przez: - Monitoring zoonoz i AMR (Antimicrobial Resistance) – Włochy mają jedne z najwyższych współczynników AMR w UE. - Badania nad wpływem zanieczyszczenia powietrza (Dolina Padu) na zdrowie układu oddechowego dzieci.

docs.title: 3.2 Planetary Health – Specyfika Śródziemnomorska
docs.text:
• Dieta Śródziemnomorska: Promowana jako model Planetary Health (niski ślad węglowy, wysokie korzyści zdrowotne).
  • Zmiany klimatu: Włochy są "hotspotem" klimatycznym; edukacja o nowych zagrożeniach (fale upałów, inwazyjne gatunki komarów np. Tygrysi, choroby takie jak West Nile).

docs.title: 4. FAQ
docs.text:
P: Dlaczego we Włoszech nie ma obowiązkowej edukacji seksualnej? O: Główną barierą jest wpływ Kościoła Katolickiego oraz silny opór partii konserwatywnych, które postrzegają taką edukację jako ingerencję w prawo rodziców do wychowania dzieci. Prawo 194 (aborcja) jest akceptowane, ale edukacja o antykoncepcji w szkołach pozostaje tematem tabu.

P: Jak "Educazione Civica" wpłynęła na EZ? O: Wprowadziła zdrowie do curriculum jako obowiązek obywatelski (33h rocznie przedmiotu), co dało nauczycielom ramy prawne do poruszania tematów dobrostanu, ale realna jakość zajęć zależy od przygotowania kadry (brak specjalistów "Health Education").

P: Czy Włochy mają problem z aktywnością fizyczną młodzieży? O: Tak, dane HBSC (<10% spełniających normy WHO) są jednymi z najgorszych w Europie. Wiąże się to ze stylem życia "sedentaria" (siedzącym) oraz infrastrukturą szkolną, która często nie zachęca do sportu poza lekcjami WF.

docs.title: Repubblica Italiana – Educazione alla Salute: Quadro Legale e Contesto (2019–2025)
1.1 Dane Podstawowe
docs.text: Parametr Wartość Kraj Włochy / Italia (IT) Populacja ~58,9 miliona (2024; starzejące się społeczeństwo) Języki urzędowe Włoski System edukacji Scentralizowany (Ministero) z silną autonomią szkół (Autonomia scolastica) Scuola primaria 5 lat (6–11 lat) Scuola secondaria I grado 3 lata (11–14 lat; tzw. "media") Scuola secondaria II grado 5 lat (14–19 lat; Liceo, Istituto Tecnico/Professionale) Organ curriculumowy MIM (Ministero dell'Istruzione e del Merito) Badania zdrowotne HBSC Italia (Istituto Superiore di Sanità – ISS)

docs.title: 1.2 Kontekst Polityczny: Rząd Meloni i "Wartości Tradycyjne"
docs.text: Włochy pod rządami koalicji prawicowej (Fratelli d'Italia, Lega, Forza Italia) kładą duży nacisk na: - Merito (Zasługi): Zmiana nazwy ministerstwa na Ministerstwo Edukacji i Zasługi (MIM). - Rodzina: Promocja tradycyjnego modelu rodziny; sceptycyzm wobec "ideologii gender" (teoria del gender). - Bezpieczeństwo: "Wychowanie do relacji" jako odpowiedź na falę femicydów (przypadek Giulii Cecchettin, 2023).

docs.title: 2.1 Educazione Civica (Ustawa 92/2019) – Główny Nośnik EZ
docs.text: Od roku szkolnego 2020/2021 Educazione Civica stała się obowiązkowym przedmiotem poprzecznym (33 godziny rocznie): - Trzy filary: 1. Konstytucja, 2. Rozwój zrównoważony, 3. Obywatelstwo cyfrowe. - Zdrowie w filarze 2: Obejmuje edukację żywieniową, profilaktykę uzależnień, dobrostan psychofizyczny oraz edukację drogową. - Reforma Valditara (DM 183/2024): Nowe wytyczne kładą większy nacisk na "poczucie przynależności narodowej" i "odpowiedzialność indywidualną" w dbaniu o zdrowie.

docs.title: 2.2 Wytyczne "Educazione alla Salute" (Ministerstwo Zdrowia & Edukacji)
docs.text: Edukacja zdrowotna nie jest osobnym przedmiotem akademickim, lecz jest oceniana w ramach Educazione Civica oraz integrowana w: - Scienze (Nauki przyrodnicze): Anatomia, fizjologia, choroby zakaźne, reprodukcja (biologicznie). - Scienze motorie e sportive (WF): Aktywność fizyczna, higiena, fair play. - P projects (PTOF): Szkoły mają autonomię (PTOF – Piano Triennale dell'Offerta Formativa) do realizowania projektów z lokalnymi ASL (Azienda Sanitaria Locale).

docs.title: 2.3 "Educare alle relazioni" (2023/2024)
docs.text: Po fali femicydów w 2023 r., Minister Valditara wprowadził projekt "Educare alle relazioni": - Cel: Przeciwdziałanie przemocy wobec kobiet, edukacja afektywna. - Kontrowersje: Grupy konserwatywne obawiały się wprowadzenia "ideologii gender". W rezultacie program jest często oparty na grupach dyskusyjnych prowadzonych przez nauczycieli-moderatorów, a nie na systematycznej edukacji seksualnej (Comprehensive Sexuality Education). - Status: Projekty są często fakultatywne i zależą od decyzji dyrektorów szkół.

docs.title: 3. Aborcja i Prawa Reprodukcyjne (Ustawa 194/1978)
docs.text: Włochy to kraj o specyficznej sytuacji "prawa vs. rzeczywistość", podobnie jak Chorwacja:

docs.title: 3.1 Legge 194/1978
docs.text:
• Aborcja jest legalna na żądanie do 90 dni (ok. 12-13 tygodni).
  • Po 90 dniach: tylko w przypadku zagrożenia życia matki lub ciężkich wad płodu.

docs.title: 3.2 Obiezione di Coscienza (Sprzeciw Sumienia)
docs.text:
• Problem systemowy: Ogromna liczba lekarzy (ginekologów) deklaruje sprzeciw sumienia.
  • Dane: Średnia krajowa to ok. 64-67% ginekologów-obiektorów, ale w regionach południowych (Molise, Basilicata, Sycylia) wskaźnik ten przekracza 80-90%.
  • Skutek: Dostęp do aborcji jest skrajnie utrudniony; kobiety muszą podróżować między regionami.

docs.title: 4. Edukacja Seksualna – Status Quo
docs.text:
• Brak obowiązku: Włochy pozostają jednym z niewielu dużych krajów UE (obok Cypru, Bułgarii, Litwy, Rumunii i Polski do niedawna), w których nie ma obowiązkowej edukacji seksualnej w szkołach na szczeblu krajowym.
  • Inicjatywy oddolne: Zależą od dobrej woli dyrekcji i współpracy z lokalnymi poradniami (Consultori Familiari).
  • Opór: Silny wpływ Watykanu oraz partii konserwatywnych blokuje każdą próbę wprowadzenia ujednoliconego programu "Sexual Health".

docs.title: 5. Kluczowe Instytucje
docs.text: Instytucja Rola MIM Ministerstwo Edukacji i Zasługi; wytyczne programowe. Ministero della Salute Ministerstwo Zdrowia; kampanie profilaktyczne (np. "Fertility Day" – kontrowersyjny). ISS Istituto Superiore di Sanità; monitoring HBSC, epidemiologia. Consultori Familiari Publiczne poradnie rodzinne; główne źródło EZ poza szkołą. ASL Lokalne jednostki zdrowia; współpracują ze szkołami przy projektach.

docs.title: 6. Źródła i Bibliografia
docs.text:
1. MIM (2024). Linee guida per l'insegnamento dell'Educazione Civica (DM 183/2024). Roma.
  2. Gazzetta Ufficiale (1978). Legge 22 maggio 1978, n. 194 - Norme per la tutela sociale della maternità e sull'interruzione volontaria della gravidanza.
  3. ISS (2024). Rapporto HBSC Italia 2022: Salute e benessere degli adolescenti. Epicentro.
  4. Ministero della Salute (2023). Relazione annuale sull'attuazione della Legge 194/78.
  5. wecanjob.it (2024). Educazione alla salute nelle scuole: il quadro normativo.

docs.text:
Sistema di educazione alla salute / Health Education System: Educazione civica (integra salute e relazioni); Biologia; nessun soggetto autonomo di educazione alla salute Bioregion: Mediterranean / Alpine Reform Status: Legge 92/2019 (Educazione civica reform); ongoing debates; Meloni government conservative influence 2022–

Questo registro elenca tutti i documenti fonte identificati per l'Italia nel progetto OneHealth EU. This registry lists all source documents identified for Italy in the OneHealth EU project.

docs.title: System Overview
docs.text: Italy has a partially centralised education system managed by the Ministero dell'Istruzione e del Merito (MIM). There is no standalone health education subject in Italian schools. Health education is delivered through: (1) Educazione civica (Civic Education — mandatory since 2019, includes health as a theme), (2) Biologia (Biology — primary carrier for sexual and physical health content), and (3) optional school projects. The Meloni government (from 2022) has taken a conservative stance on sexuality education, opposing gender theory and emphasising traditional family values. The ISS (Istituto Superiore di Sanità) is the key health data and policy body.

docs.title: 1. Legge 20 agosto 2019, n. 92 — Introduzione dell'insegnamento scolastico dell'educazione civica
docs.text:
• Titolo completo / Full title: Legge 20 agosto 2019, n. 92 — Introduzione dell'insegnamento scolastico dell'educazione civica
  • Type: Act of Parliament / Legge | Year: 2019
  • Publisher: Parlamento italiano / Gazzetta Ufficiale
  • Description: Reintroduces Educazione civica as a mandatory subject (min. 33 hours/year) in all Italian schools from primary to upper secondary. One of the three pillars is sustainable development and environmental education, which includes health, wellbeing, and One Health themes. The other two pillars cover the Constitution and digital citizenship.
  • Access (normattiva.it): https://www.normattiva.it/uri-res/N2Ls?urn:nir:stato:legge:2019-08-20;92

docs.title: 2. Linee guida per l'insegnamento dell'educazione civica — MIM 2020 (and 2024 update)
docs.text:
• Type: Ministerial guidelines / Linee guida | Year: 2020 (base); 2024 (update)
  • Publisher: Ministero dell'Istruzione (now MIM)
  • Description: Official guidelines implementing the 2019 Educazione civica law. Include health-related content requirements under the sustainability pillar. The 2024 update by the Meloni government modified some content emphases.
  • Access (MIM): https://www.mim.gov.it/educazione-civica
